chapter: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
title: Tyree Glenn and Sultry Serenade
summary: Brown describes Tyree Glenn on vibes and wa-wa trombone and his tune Sultry Serenade.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: (Inaudible) -- '46 and into '47. And then it was in '47 that Tyree joined, about the time that --
Oh, yes. Tyree. That's right.
Tyree was in trombone and what you call his electrical appliance, remember?
He played vibraphones.
Well, that's what Duke called his vibes. He used to introduce Tyree -- and now Tyree Glen and his electrical appliance.
Yeah.
And Tyree was playing the -- was he playing the wa-wa trombone --
Yes.
-- at the beginning?
Yes. He was very good at that too.
(inaudible). I remember him on "My Sue" --
Uh-huh.
And several numbers which --
He was a good man, very good man. Everybody seemed to come in and fit, and they did their stint. And when they left they were missed.
Tyree did some writing too.
Well, as most of us did. Oh, he wrote a tune. Yes. Yes. He did write a tune. I've forgotten the name of it right now.
The one that was recorded with Duke was recorded as "Sultry Serenade".
"Sultry Serenade" that's it.
And when Tyree first wrote it, he wrote it during the war in Germany, and he called it Working Eyes.
Yes. Uh-huh.
And then he played it for Duke, and Duke retitled it "Sultry Serenade" and recorded it, and I took co-composer think that (inaudible) the credit.
Uh-huh.
And then it was -- the name was changed again to "How could you do a thing like that to me" when I think Ella recorded it --
Oh, yes.
When and it acquired a lyric. But I thought Tyree did some other writing too besides that one number.
Now, I didn't know of too much of his writing ability. I knew that he was very good playing.
And there was somebody named Ted Kelly. That was brief.
I'm Don't trying to remember him.
